lab_title: DNA Structure and Semiconservative Replication: A 3D Exploration
top_level_objectives: Understand the three-dimensional structure of the DNA double helix and its key components
Identify and explain complementary base pairing rules and hydrogen bonding patterns
Explain the antiparallel nature of DNA strands and its relationship to directionality (5' to 3')
Visualize and describe the mechanism of semiconservative DNA replication
Connect the antiparallel structure to the asymmetric synthesis of leading and lagging strands

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce students to the overall three-dimensional structure of DNA and its major anatomical components.
key_visuals: A complete DNA double helix displayed in 3D space, rotating slowly to show the spiral geometry
The two sugar-phosphate backbones highlighted in contrasting colors (e.g., blue and orange)
Nitrogenous bases clearly visible projecting inward from the backbones
student_actions: Examine the DNA helix from multiple angles by rotating it in AR space
Identify and label the sugar-phosphate backbones and the nitrogenous bases
Observe how the bases lie perpendicular to the axis of the helix

scenes.brief_purpose: Examine the specific rules of complementary base pairing and the hydrogen bonding patterns that stabilize the helix.
key_visuals: A zoomed-in cross-sectional view of the DNA helix showing 3-4 base pairs
Adenine-thymine pairs with two hydrogen bonds displayed as dashed lines
Guanine-cytosine pairs with three hydrogen bonds displayed as dashed lines
Color-coding of the four bases to distinguish them clearly
student_actions: Identify which bases pair with which by matching them across the helix
Count the number of hydrogen bonds in each base pair type
Predict what bases would pair with a given template sequence
Recognize that base pairing is always purine-to-pyrimidine

scenes.brief_purpose: Clarify the antiparallel orientation of the two strands and the 5' to 3' directionality that defines DNA polarity.
key_visuals: One complete DNA strand with 5' and 3' ends clearly labeled and color-highlighted
The complementary strand showing opposite directionality (3' to 5' relative to the first strand)
Arrows or visual indicators showing the direction along each backbone
The sugar-phosphate backbone structure with the 5' carbon of deoxyribose and the 3' carbon clearly marked
student_actions: Trace the path of each strand from 5' to 3' end
Explain why the strands must run antiparallel to allow base pairing
Predict the 3' to 5' orientation of a strand given the 5' to 3' orientation of its complement
Observe how antiparallel orientation affects the geometry of the helix

scenes.scene_name: DNA Replication Initiation and Helicase Action
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the beginning of DNA replication by showing how helicase unwinds the double helix at the replication fork.
key_visuals: A DNA double helix with a replication fork visible
Helicase enzyme approaching and binding to the replication fork
The double helix unwinding in front of helicase as hydrogen bonds between bases break
Single-strand binding (SSB) proteins coating the exposed single strands to prevent re-annealing
The exposed template strands color-differentiated to show their 3' to 5' orientation
student_actions: Observe the breaking of hydrogen bonds as helicase unwinds the helix
Identify where SSB proteins bind and explain their role
Note which template strand runs 3' to 5' in the direction of the replication fork (the leading strand template) and which runs 5' to 3' (the lagging strand template)

scenes.brief_purpose: Show continuous synthesis of the leading strand, highlighting how DNA polymerase reads the 3' to 5' template and synthesizes 5' to 3'.
key_visuals: A replication fork with the leading strand template (3' to 5' orientation) visible
DNA polymerase III enzyme actively synthesizing the new leading strand
The growing 5' to 3' DNA strand being extended in the direction of the replication fork
Nucleotides being added one at a time to the 3'-OH group of the growing strand
Continuous, uninterrupted synthesis progressing along the template
student_actions: Follow the synthesis direction of the new strand (5' to 3')
Explain why leading strand synthesis is continuous
Identify the template strand orientation and predict how it aligns with polymerase movement
Observe that polymerase moves along the template in the 3' to 5' direction

scenes.scene_name: Lagging Strand Synthesis and Okazaki Fragments
scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate discontinuous synthesis of the lagging strand, explaining why Okazaki fragments form and how they are joined.
key_visuals: The same replication fork showing the lagging strand template (5' to 3' orientation)
Multiple DNA polymerase enzymes synthesizing short Okazaki fragments (approximately 1000-2000 nucleotides in prokaryotes) in the 5' to 3' direction, but oriented away from the replication fork
RNA primers visible at the 5' end of each Okazaki fragment
DNA ligase enzyme joining adjacent Okazaki fragments by sealing the nick between them
A fully synthesized lagging strand showing no visible fragment boundaries after ligation
student_actions: Explain why lagging strand synthesis is discontinuous by considering the antiparallel geometry
Identify each Okazaki fragment and its orientation relative to the replication fork
Predict where new Okazaki fragments will form as replication progresses
Observe the role of DNA ligase in connecting fragments into a continuous strand

scenes.scene_name: Semiconservative Replication and Daughter DNA Molecules
scenes.brief_purpose: Show the completion of DNA replication and reveal the semiconservative nature of the process, with each daughter molecule containing one original and one new strand.
key_visuals: The original parental DNA double helix with the two strands color-coded distinctly (e.g., original 'parental' strand in one color, newly synthesized strands in another)
The replication process completing, with both daughter DNA molecules visible
Each daughter molecule clearly showing one original parental strand paired with one newly synthesized strand
Side-by-side comparison emphasizing that both daughter molecules are identical to the original and to each other
Optional: A label or annotation showing the distribution of old vs. new DNA in each daughter molecule
student_actions: Identify which strands in each daughter molecule are original parental DNA and which are newly synthesized
Explain what 'semiconservative' means in the context of DNA replication
Verify that each daughter molecule is chemically and genetically identical to the parent
Reflect on how the antiparallel structure and directional constraints of DNA polymerase made asymmetric synthesis necessary and thus semiconservative replication inevitable
